titre: The Letter Victor Hugo Never Sent
accroche: A “?”, a “!”: the shortest exchange in literary history never took place, and was already circulating twelve years before Les Misérables.
contenu_vulgarise:
The anecdote turns up in every collection of literary quotations. In 1862, away on vacation during the publication of *Les Misérables*, Victor Hugo supposedly grew anxious about the novel's success and wrote to his publisher a letter containing a single character: “?”. The reply, just as laconic: “!”. Two punctuation marks, and an entire commercial plot summed up. The story is too good to be true, and it is not.

## What the Investigation Reveals

The American site Quote Investigator, which specializes in tracking down apocryphal quotations and anecdotes, traced the trail back to a source well before Hugo. As early as April 1850, an English newspaper, the *Nottinghamshire Guardian*, already published the same story, with no author's name, and with a variant: the first sign is indeed a question mark, but the second is a zero, a figure meaning “nothing to report.” The anecdote then circulates throughout the 1850s in the British press, the *Birmingham Journal*, the *Nottingham Review*, the *Hampshire Advertiser*, *The Observer*, then in the American press, staying anonymous each time it is retold. Only one variant departs from this, in 1854 in the *Portland Weekly Advertiser*. It gives the story protagonists, and they are not writers: “an American merchant” and “his agent in London.”

*Les Misérables* appears in 1862. But it is only in 1892, thirty years later, that the anecdote attaches itself to Hugo for the first time, in a collection published in Philadelphia by William S. Walsh, the *Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities*. It is Walsh who, in passing, turns the original zero into an exclamation point, giving the story its definitive form and its most memorable punch line.

## Why This Kind of Story Travels So Well

An anecdote without an author never dies: it looks for a host. The more prestigious the host, the better the line circulates: people do not gladly tell that an unknown man was witty, they prefer it to be a giant of letters. Hugo, in 1892, ticks every box: dead for seven years, already turned into a statue, famous enough to make any witticism attributed to him credible. The same mechanism later pinned a variant of the same story on Oscar Wilde, which appeared in 2013, one hundred twenty-one years after Walsh.

## What It Shifts

The anecdote is false, and instructive about how apocryphal quotations are born, the very ones that a project like this one undertakes never to reproduce. A plausible sentence, an illustrious name, no verifiable primary source: the recipe that produces a “letter from Hugo” is exactly the one that produces any false quotation attributed to Einstein or Churchill. The only antidote remains the same: trace it back to the oldest document, and see what it really says.

repere.texte: The first known version of the story appears in April 1850 in the Nottinghamshire Guardian, anonymously, twelve years before the publication of Les Misérables. It is attributed to Victor Hugo only in 1892, in a collection by William S. Walsh.
repere.source: Quote Investigator, “Briefest Correspondence: Question Mark? Exclamation Mark!”, 2014

carte.punch: “?” “!”: the exchange between Victor Hugo and his publisher never took place.
carte.idee: The anecdote has it that Victor Hugo sent a question mark to his publisher to ask how Les Misérables was selling, and received an exclamation point in return. It was already circulating, anonymously, twelve years before the novel's publication, and was attributed to Hugo only in 1892.

quiz.question: How did the anecdote of the “?”/“!” letter end up being attributed to Victor Hugo?
choix: Hugo told it himself in a letter to his publisher, found after his death
A literary critic invented it in 1930 to illustrate the novel's success
A collection of literary anecdotes from 1892 took up an anonymous story published as early as 1850 and attached it to Hugo
The archives of the publisher Hurst and Blackett hold the original letter
quiz.explication: No letter from Hugo, no publisher's archive: the anecdote already existed, anonymously, in the British press of 1850, even before the publication of Les Misérables. It is William S. Walsh who, in a collection of 1892, attaches it to Hugo for the first time, and turns the final sign, originally a zero, into an exclamation point.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What variant of the story appears as early as April 1850 in the Nottinghamshire Guardian?
choix: The two signs are a question mark and an exclamation point, as in the known version
The story features a French publisher and his printer
The story already attributes the anecdote to an anonymous English writer
The first sign is a question mark, the second a zero meaning “nothing to report”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1850 version is anonymous and gives a zero as the second sign, meaning “nothing to report,” rather than the exclamation point of the version popularized later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who are the protagonists of the only variant of the anecdote that departs from the usual format, in 1854?
choix: A ship's captain and his first mate, in a maritime story
An American merchant and his agent in London
A journalist and his editor-in-chief in New York
A professor and his pupil, in an educational anecdote
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1854, the Portland Weekly Advertiser gives different protagonists, not writers, but “an American merchant” and “his agent in London.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other famous writer later had a variant of the same anecdote attributed to him?
choix: Oscar Wilde, in a version that appeared in 2013
Mark Twain, in a letter published after his death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The same mechanism of attribution to a prestigious author later pinned a variant of the same story on Oscar Wilde, which appeared in 2013.
